q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE AS C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT AS D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR AS I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(I.SALARY) > 100 AND MAX(I.SALARY) < 75
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE AS C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT AS D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR AS I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(I.SALARY) >= 100 AND MAX(I.SALARY) < 75

q2_prompt_sql: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE AS C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT AS D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR AS I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(I.SALARY) >= 100 AND MAX(I.SALARY) < 75
counterexample: INSERT INTO DEPARTMENT (DEPT_NAME) VALUES ('CS'); INSERT INTO INSTRUCTOR (ID, SALARY, DEPT_NAME) VALUES (1, 50, 'CS'), (2, 50, 'CS');
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because the HAVING clause in Q1 uses '>' for the sum of salaries, while Q2 uses '>='. This difference can lead to different results, especially if the sum of salaries is exactly 100.
counterexample_dsp: A department with an exact sum of 100 in instructor salaries and a maximum salary less than 75.
